claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy is an ordered, single-phase hexagonal material.
This FeMnNiGeSi alloy undergoes a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Conventional arc-melted or melt-spun FeMnNiGeSi samples have relatively large grains.
Conventional arc-melted or melt-spun FeMnNiGeSi samples have a low surface-to-volume ratio.
The distribution and density of grain boundaries govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of the FeMnNiGeSi alloy.
Reducing the deposition cooling rate or adjusting substrate temperature will refine the grains and increase the density of nanoscale grain boundaries.
Grain boundaries provide heterogeneous nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transformation.
Increasing grain-boundary density lowers and broadens the effective distribution of transformation energy barriers.
A broader transformation-barrier distribution produces a smoother and more gradual phase transition.
Increasing grain-boundary density reduces magnetic or thermal hysteresis.
Increasing grain-boundary density broadens the temperature range of the magnetocaloric transition.
Grain refinement may slightly reduce the peak magnetic entropy change.
Despite a possible reduction in peak entropy change, grain refinement will improve overall refrigerant capacity.
The increased interface area associated with greater grain-boundary density promotes faster heat exchange.

The predictions are restricted to non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys retaining an ordered single-phase structure and a first-order magnetostructural transition under low applied fields near the transition temperature.
The intervention is tested at fixed composition so that grain size and grain-boundary density are the principal varied factors.
Failure of increased grain-boundary density to significantly reduce hysteresis and broaden the transition would falsify the proposed microstructural mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial state and baseline group arc-melted ingots and melt-spun products together as 'as-deposited' materials, whereas the intervention is framed as thin-film deposition using a substrate temperature. These are not clearly matched processing routes or specimen geometries, so the proposed comparison does not consistently define the baseline.

The baseline attributes limited heat exchange to low external surface-to-volume ratio, but the mechanism invokes increased internal grain-boundary area as if it directly increased heat-exchange area. Internal interfacial area and external area available to the cooling medium are distinct quantities.
